title: The Ending — A Pencil in His Hand
subtitle: Three possible futures

lines.text: First. Aarav takes the scholarship. He studies engineering, discovers new capacities, builds a life he could not have imagined from inside the repair shop. His preferences change because he has finally been exposed to the alternative. This is learning — genuine, experience-based revision.

Second. He takes it, struggles, and returns to repair work. Not in defeat — in knowledge. He has seen both lives from the inside and chosen the one that fits. The preference for the shop is now informed, not assumed.

Third. He declines after honest reflection. He chooses his craft, his family, a life shaped by values he has deliberately examined. This is not adaptation. It is a considered decision about what kind of life he wants to lead.
Which future is best? I cannot answer that by comparing incomes or degrees. And I should not answer it by assuming that more education is automatically a better life.

shots.card:
The ethical question was never
"Should Aarav become an engineer?"

lines.text: The ethical question was never "Should Aarav become an engineer?"
It was: Does he have a genuine opportunity to decide — and have the conditions around him allowed that decision to be truly his?

A just society does not make people content by narrowing what they dare to want. It expands the conditions under which people form and exercise their choices — and then respects what they choose, even when they choose differently from what we would have chosen for them.
Elster does not argue that every change in preference is irrational. He argues that we must examine how preferences are formed before treating their satisfaction as proof that all is well.
Sen does not argue that freedom replaces happiness. He argues that happiness alone is too narrow a window through which to see a life.
Together, they leave us with a question that has no comfortable answer:
When we give someone the freedom to choose, who gets to decide what freedom should look like?
